claims.text: The initial high-entropy alloy is homogeneous and single-phase, with no significant pre-existing grain-boundary segregation or intermetallic particles.
High-temperature service exposure causes nanoscale grain-boundary segregation of selected alloying elements.
The segregating elements migrate preferentially because they diffuse faster along grain boundaries.
Grain-boundary segregation produces local compositional fluctuations.
The local compositional fluctuations reduce grain-boundary cohesive strength.
Reduced grain-boundary cohesion causes early crack initiation and brittle intergranular fracture.
The proposed embrittlement occurs without overt, large-scale grain-boundary precipitates.
Conventional-alloy brittle behavior is driven by coarse grain-boundary precipitates rather than subtle segregation.
Annealed samples will have lower fracture toughness or fracture strain than baseline samples.
Annealed samples will exhibit more brittle, intergranular fracture features than baseline samples.
The reduction in toughness will correlate with localized grain-boundary compositional changes.
Uniformly distributed alloying elements in the initial single-phase microstructure provide high fracture toughness and ductility.
A temperature range exists that activates grain-boundary diffusion while remaining below complete phase transformation or large-scale coarsening.
The proposed mechanism is relevant to high-entropy alloys used in tough, high-temperature engineering applications.

contradictions.description: The conditions specify high-temperature annealing under uniaxial loading, whereas the experiment makes stress assistance optional and otherwise describes mechanical loading only after treatment, leaving the role and timing of applied stress inconsistent.
